name: Uma Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms or government, and we keep your answers confidential. What is an ordinary workday for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and lead the product-label review team at a large food company. We check ingredient changes, translate the legal requirements into instructions for designers, and stop a print run if a label is wrong. I have an MBA and know the approval chain better than most people here, but I’ve never used an AI tool; I prefer to see the source myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what is your situation outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like catching a mistake before thousands of cartons go out. I earn about the usual pay for this role and have roughly three months of expenses saved, though my apartment rent rises each year. I live alone, and there are some other management jobs nearby, but few with this mix of labels and production.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the label team AI Plateau sounds like a faster way to sort routine documents, not a reason to skip our sign-off. We can still walk a changed carton to the factory floor and check the printed version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job would stay. A small sorting tool might remove dull filing, but the rent keeps climbing while pay is ordinary. I do not want to be the person who approves a wrong allergen line because a screen looked tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the two-person label check and put the latest ingredient sheet beside every approval. If a basic sorter arrives, I’d ask the print supervisor to show me ten real examples before letting it file our records. I would leave my three-month reserve alone unless a bill requires it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the job, though rent is always on my mind. A filing shortcut is not a reason to change my whole life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would persuade you to use the sorter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten records with the correct old and new versions attached. I would compare them myself and ask where a rejected record goes. If the answer is vague, the team keeps the paper trail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why two people on every label?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One person checks the words and the other checks the actual pack. Last month the file was right but the printer used an older plate. A filing tool would not catch an old printer plate until someone stood by the cartons.

say: **Routine sorting** may speed records, but the label team must still sign off.
A real carton needs a **floor check** before release.
think: My **job** looks steady if AI only handles filing.
A wrong **allergen line** is a bigger risk than slow paperwork.
do: **Keep** the two-person label and carton check throughout 2026.
**Compare** ten real records before approving any basic sorter after arrival.
feel: I feel **calm** about work, with rent still on my mind.
S0.quote: A filing tool would not catch an old printer plate until someone stood by the cartons.
fieldNote: Her **three-month reserve** gives room for ordinary rent pressure, while her job appears stable in this mild picture.
She insists on **physical proof** from the factory floor before trusting a filing shortcut.

steps.text: Keep two-person checks of ingredient wording and printed cartons

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will write and check many documents before we print anything. I’d ask the company to tell us which decisions still need a named person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, draft instructions and version comparisons take a large part of my week. If the system does those, the company might need fewer managers. I am good at stopping a bad launch, but I can see my team shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I’d make a log of label errors caught by people and ask the plant manager to review it at the next production meeting. If an AI checking system is introduced, I’d sit through the company’s paid demonstration and test it on old rejected labels before approving any use. I would keep rent spending within my present budget rather than buy new furniture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious. Three months of savings helps, but I could still be cut from the label team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error belongs in that log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A designer changed the nut warning while fixing the font size last week. Our second checker noticed it before plates were made. I would include the cost of reprinting if we had missed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train on the system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch the paid demonstration and test its output. I am not agreeing to learn a new job until the company shows what the system gets wrong and who signs the final label. That is my line.

say: **AI checks** need a named human decision before cartons print.
I’d show managers the **label errors** people caught.
think: Drafting and version checks take much of my week and could **shrink my team**.
My **three-month reserve** buys time, not a permanent job.
do: **Log** human-caught label errors for the next production meeting.
**Test** a company checking system on rejected labels after its paid demonstration.
**Delay** furniture purchases while keeping rent inside the current budget.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a smaller team despite some savings.
S1.quote: Three months of savings helps, but I could still be cut from the label team.
fieldNote: She separates a **paid demonstration** from committing to retrain; her plan is to inspect a proposed system.
Her **error log** argues for human sign-off with a specific nut-warning mistake, while she privately fears headcount cuts.

steps.text: Log human-caught label errors for the next production meeting
Test the proposed checker on rejected labels before approving use
Delay buying new furniture to protect the rent budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 leaves very little time for the company to decide who carries responsibility for labels. I would ask for a written plan before the next print contract is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cheap thinking work could do our drafts, comparisons and schedules by 2028. Robots on the factory floor around 2031 would arrive later, but my desk work would already be exposed. I expect several jobs in my team to go and cannot rule out mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I’d speak with the plant manager about the cut timetable and apply for the vacant quality lead post at a nearby drinks maker if the listed salary matches mine. I’d also save another month of expenses from my wages during 2027, on top of the three-month reserve, if my pay continues. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my post ends, I’d take that quality role if offered, not wait for a title that sounds grander.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. I can cover a short gap, but losing the job while rent rises would eat the reserve quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say in that meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask who signs a recalled label and when staff will know which posts are ending. A date matters more than reassurance. I want to tell the team what I actually know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the drinks maker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Their quality lead post includes factory checks and supplier calls. I know those parts, but I do not know whether the vacancy will stay open or whether the salary is real. I would confirm both before leaving.

say: **AGI by 2028** needs a written responsibility and staffing plan before new print contracts.
I’d tell the team only the **dates** I can verify.
think: My drafts and comparisons could go in **2028**, before factory robots around 2031.
I expect **team cuts** and might lose my own post.
do: **Ask** the plant manager next week for cut dates and recall responsibility.
**Apply** for the nearby quality lead vacancy if salary is comparable.
**Save** another month of expenses from wages in 2027 if pay continues.
feel: I feel **alarmed** that rent could consume my reserve after job loss.
S2.quote: A date matters more than reassurance.
fieldNote: Her **quality application** depends on a live vacancy and comparable salary; she does not assume another job is guaranteed.
The **2028 thinking shock** reaches her desk before robots reach the factory around 2031.

steps.text: Apply for the drinks maker quality lead vacancy if salary matches
Save another month of expenses from 2027 wages if pay continues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives the company time to decide how label checks and recalls work together. I’d want that process tested in real production, not only on old files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to find a role closer to factory quality while I still earn. The desk comparisons could go in 2031; capable robots on the line come around 2034. I might be safer overseeing recalls, but that role could change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask to shadow the recall coordinator for one shift a month and keep a record of the decisions I can make without software. If a paid recall rotation opens next year, I’d take it after checking that my salary stays the same. Once AGI arrives around 2031, I’d apply for an internal recall lead post if it still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, though less pressed than in the two-year version. A real rotation would let me find out what I can do before making a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on a recall shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How the coordinator finds the affected batch, phones shops and decides whether to stop other lines. I know the label record; I do not yet know the whole recall chain. I would write down the gaps after each shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the rotation cuts your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not take it. My rent is affordable now because I have ordinary pay and a reserve, and I will not trade those for a possible future opening. I would keep shadowing if the manager allows it.

say: **Five years** allows factory testing of the label and recall process.
I’d want real **production evidence**, not only old files.
think: Desk comparison work could end in **2031**, before line robots around 2034.
A recall lead role might be **safer**, but its future is uncertain.
do: **Shadow** the recall coordinator monthly from 2026 if my manager approves.
**Take** a paid recall rotation only if salary stays level.
**Apply** for an internal recall lead post after 2031 if it exists.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time for a measured workplace trial.
S3.quote: I know the label record; I do not yet know the whole recall chain.
fieldNote: She prefers a **monthly shadow** and a salary-protected rotation over a sudden career change.
Her confidence in **recall work** is tentative because the role may also change with AI.

steps.text: Shadow the recall coordinator monthly if the manager approves
Take the paid recall rotation only if salary stays the same
Apply for an internal recall lead vacancy after 2031 if available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2036 should give us a decade to run better label checks and make honest career decisions. Management should publish the roles and pay rather than a vague training catalogue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could let me build a larger reserve and become a quality manager if a real opening appears. My desk checks still face AGI around 2036, and factory robots follow around 2039. I do not see a reason to leave a solid job this year on a prediction alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d continue the two-person sign-off and add a fixed amount to savings each payday if rent allows. I’d review quality vacancies every six months and take a paid factory-quality rotation if the company offers one without a pay cut. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for a quality manager role if it still has real authority and a salary at least equal to mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than frightened. A decade gives me room, provided the company tells the truth about vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check whether the role has authority?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask who can stop a print run and who signs a recall. A quality manager title without power to stop a print run would be decoration. I have seen enough decorative titles in this company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if rent rises again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fixed savings amount would shrink first. I would not count money in an account before it is there. I can keep the current job and revisit the plan after the lease renewal.

say: A **decade** should bring published roles, pay and tested label checks.
A **quality manager** needs real authority to stop bad print runs.
think: I could build **savings** and move into quality management if an opening appears.
My desk work remains exposed in **2036**, before factory robots around 2039.
do: **Add** a fixed amount to savings each payday if rent permits.
**Take** a paid factory-quality rotation only without a pay cut.
feel: I feel **uneasy** until vacancies and authority are clear.
S4.quote: A quality manager title without power to stop a print run would be decoration.
fieldNote: She ties a **long runway** to real authority, salary protection and the next rent renewal.
The **savings amount** remains conditional rather than counted as money already available.

steps.text: Add a fixed amount to savings each payday if rent permits
Take a paid factory-quality rotation only without a pay cut
Review quality manager vacancies every six months

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a team cut could reach my post before I find another. A written staffing timetable and a salary-protected quality opening would help. I can cover a short gap, not a year of rising rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is allowed to stop the press when the AI approves a wrong label. A food company can automate label checks, but it still needs a name on the stop order. That is where the risk lands.

headlineQuote: A food company can automate label checks, but it still needs a name on the stop order.
portrait: **Uma, 27**, leads product-label review at a large food company and has an MBA.
She earns **typical pay**, has about three months saved and sees some nearby management openings.
She has never used **AI tools** and insists on source documents and printed cartons before approving labels.
She moves from **calm** in AI Plateau to alarm by 2028, then tests recall work with more notice.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her team and consume her rent reserve before another quality job appears.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing timetable** and a salary-protected quality opening would help her plan.
